Essential trace minerals are vital for general human health and athletic performance. Zinc (Zn) plays critical roles in several biochemical processes in exercise physiology, especially during intense physical exercise. This research aimed to analyze erythrocyte, platelet, plasma and urine Zn concentrations among men’s and female soccer players over a sports season. A total of 22 male soccer players (20.61 ± 2.66 years; 71.50 ± 5.93 kg) and 24 female soccer players (23.37 ± 3.95 years; 59.58 ± 7.17 kg) participated in this longitudinal quasi-experimental study. Three assessments were carried out over the season: 1st evaluation: first week of training (August); 2nd assessment: middle of the season, between the end of the first and second round (January) and 3rd assessment: last week of training (May/June). In all evaluations extracellular (plasma and urine) and intracellular (erythrocytes and platelets) Zn concentrations were determined, as well as physical fitness and several blood parameters. Inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry was used to measure Zn concentrations. Plasma and urinary concentrations were higher among male soccer players ( p < 0.05) while erythrocyte and platelet Zn concentrations were higher in the female soccer players ( p < 0.05). Additionally, variations in urinary and platelet Zn concentrations were observed over the season. Introduction Zinc is found in various tissues, organs and secretions, being one of the most important trace minerals. Iron (Fe) is the only element that is higher in abundance than zinc [ 1 ]. About 95% of Zn is located inside the cells. Zn is present in all cell organelles, with 60–80% located in the cytosol and the remainder bound to cellular membranes [ 2 ]. Zn is involved in different actions of the human body during intense physical exercise and is related to muscular strength and endurance [ 3 ]. In addition, Zn acts as an antioxidant superoxide dismutase (SOD) together with Cu (Copper) [ 4 ]. At the same time, Zn provides structural stability and is involved in enzymatic activities of metalloenzymes, such as lactate dehydrogenase and carbonic anhydrase [ 5 ]. The latter is one of the most abundant enzymes in the body, being essential for maintaining the acid–base balance of body fluids [ 6 ]. Thus, this mineral plays an important role in high-intensity sports such as soccer. Long-term physical training produces different adaptations that could influence Zn redistribution [ 7 ]. This redistribution seems to depend on the type of physical exercise, training status, exercise duration and environmental temperature [ 8 ]. Soccer is a vigorous sport with great physical demands over the season [ 9 ], generating a high level of free radicals [ 10 ]; therefore the role of Zn is essential in this sport. However, Zn levels can vary over the season for different reasons. High temperatures are an element that can affect Zn levels due to its excretion through sweat, and an increased excretion of this element has been observed in urine, even in acclimated subjects [ 11 ]. In addition, soccer is an intense physical sport with a tight competition schedule, which produces higher reactive oxygen species caused by training [ 12 ]. The resulting high mitochondrial oxygen consumption and electron transport flux results in oxidative stress leading to the generation of free radicals and, as a consequence, possible lipid peroxidation [ 13 ]. Moreover, high impacts result in a greater level of muscle damage, triggering the release of Zn by muscle cells [ 8 ]. A recent study has found a connection between creatine kinase (CK) and Zn [ 14 ]. There is a high incidence of injuries in soccer [ 15 ]. In this respect, it should be noted that these impacts trigger a release of erythrocyte Zn into the plasma. This could be the reason why several studies report elevated plasma/serum Zn in top-level athletes [ 16 , 17 ]. Recent research has shown that athletes who engage in regular physical training have increased zinc levels in their plasma and decreased levels in their erythrocytes [ 17 ]. According to these findings, it is important to assess trace minerals not just in extracellular compartments, since the plasma/serum zinc concentration is a limited marker for determining zinc status in humans. The current literature usually evaluates the status of this mineral in men, and there is a lack of knowledge about the status of Zn in women athletes. It has been observed that Zn concentrations are higher in men than in women before and after a maximal incremental test [ 18 ]. In addition, it is known that Zn loss is greater in men than in women under both hyperthermic and normothermic conditions [ 19 ]. These differences are mainly explained by a greater muscle mass in men than in women, since most Zn is found in skeletal muscle [ 1 ]. Strength outputs, and thus muscle damage, are greater in men during competition, so the release of Zn into plasma is higher [ 20 ]. However, the studies that have been carried out evaluate Zn in a single matrix or at a single moment of the season. It seems necessary to establish the behavior of this mineral over the course of a season in different matrices as mentioned above. A recent study reported values of the effect of resistance training in marines [ 21 ]. Nevertheless, the kinetics of this mineral may vary depending on the type of exercise. Soccer is a mixed-mode sport. Another factor that can modify Zn kinetics are injuries, as these could cause hemolysis. In addition, it should be noted that the menstrual cycle in women can also alter the homeostasis of Zn over a season, so it would be interesting to study this element in different matrices in women and observe the differences between sexes to know the possible requirements. Therefore, this study aimed to observe Zn concentrations at different moments of the sports season in men’s and female soccer players in the following biological matrices: erythrocytes, platelets, plasma and urine. Based on previous studies [ 14 , 17 , 22 ], it could be hypothesized that there would be differences between sexes, depending on the matrix analyzed, as well as over the season due to the physical demands of the sport.

extracted_data.document_summary: This longitudinal quasi-experimental study investigated sex differences and seasonal variations in Zinc (Zn) concentrations across various biological compartments (plasma, urine, erythrocytes, and platelets) in male and female soccer players over a full sports season. The study aimed to identify physiological differences between sexes and the impact of the season, considering factors like nutritional intake, physical demands, and female hormonal status. Key findings revealed that male players exhibited higher extracellular Zn (plasma and urine), while female players showed higher intracellular Zn (erythrocytes and platelets, particularly in relative values). Additionally, variations were observed in urinary and platelet Zn concentrations over the season, with a general decrease towards the end, and muscle damage and hemolysis from training were linked to increased plasma Zn levels.

treatment_details.dose_specificity: This was a longitudinal observational study of male and female soccer players participating in a full sports season, characterized as a vigorous sport with great physical demands. Three assessments were conducted: at the beginning of training (August), mid-season (January), and end of training (May/June). Training load was reduced two days before each assessment, but no internal training load data or specific dose-response comparisons were reported. Dietary zinc intake was monitored and found to be above recommended levels in both sexes. Inherent sex differences in physical demands and match intensity (e.g., higher in men) were noted.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher in male soccer players compared to females (p < 0.05, p <= 0.01 with large effect size). This included increases potentially from muscle cells and hemolysis due to training or trauma. All observed levels were within normal concentrations.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Essential trace mineral, involved in numerous enzymatic activities (e.g., SOD, carbonic anhydrase), antioxidant defense, structural stability, acid-base balance, nitrogen absorption and retention. It is the primary extracellular compartment for Zn and is released into plasma from cells (e.g., muscle, erythrocytes) upon damage.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Observed in male soccer players during a full sports season, linked to intense physical exercise, higher physical demands, impacts, muscle damage, and hemolysis from training/matches.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates muscle damage level, hemolysis, and physiological stress from intense sport. Higher levels in males are associated with greater muscle mass, strength, and physical demands. Requires considering intracellular concentrations for complete Zn status.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher in males, with seasonal variations
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher in male soccer players compared to females (p < 0.05, p <= 0.01 with large effect size). Males showed an increase followed by a decrease over the season, while females showed an inverse pattern (decrease then increase). Overall, urinary Zn concentrations decreased at the end of the season. Significant differences were observed between assessments 1 & 3 and 2 & 3 (p <= 0.01) with a moderate sex x measurement interaction.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Involved in nitrogen absorption and retention. Its elimination from the body via urine is influenced by muscle protein catabolism, increased amino acid filtration, muscle damage, formation of Zn amino acid chelates, and environmental factors like temperature.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Observed in soccer players over a sports season, influenced by strenuous exercise, regular training, intense aerobic and strength training, post-exercise recovery, prolonged heat exposure, and sex-based physiological differences.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Higher urinary Zn in males suggests greater excretion, possibly due to higher physical demands, muscle damage, and sweat loss. Seasonal variations reflect dynamic zinc balance and adaptive mechanisms to avoid losses, indicating muscle damage levels and potential regeneration processes.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher in females, with potential seasonal decrease
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Higher concentrations observed in female soccer players compared to males (p < 0.05, p <= 0.05 with large effect size for relative values); no significant differences for absolute concentrations. A fall in erythrocyte levels was reported with a rise in plasma Zn (referencing prior study).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A major intracellular reservoir for Zn (95% of total body Zn). It is part of the erythrocyte membrane and a cofactor for SOD and carbonic anhydrase. Considered a reliable indicator of long-term Zn status, generally unaffected by short-term diet or inflammation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Observed in male and female soccer players over a sports season, with changes influenced by sex differences in muscle mass, muscle damage, hemolysis from physical training, and potential nutritional deficits.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Higher erythrocyte Zn in females suggests greater intracellular retention or lower release, possibly linked to less muscle mass or damage, or a predominantly aerobic metabolism. A fall in levels, coupled with rising plasma Zn, indicates hemolysis from physical training, thereby revealing muscle damage levels.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher in females; progressively decreased over the season
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher in female soccer players compared to males (p < 0.05, p <= 0.01 with large effect sizes for both absolute and relative values). Intraplatelet concentrations expressed in absolute values progressively decreased throughout the investigation, with differences found between assessments 1 & 3 and 2 & 3 (p <= 0.05). Significant differences were observed over the season and between sexes for relative concentrations (p <= 0.01).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Intracellular Zn storage, involved in various cellular processes and homeostasis. Platelets can release Zn into serum during the coagulation process.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Observed in male and female soccer players over a sports season, with dynamic changes related to physical demands of the sport, sex differences, and comparison to low physical activity subjects.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Highlights sex-specific differences in intracellular zinc status. Seasonal variations reflect dynamic adaptations or responses to prolonged physical training or competition, and changes could be relevant to coagulation processes and injury incidence in soccer.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Not reported in this biomarker entry
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Determined via questionnaire over three days; no observed differences in Zn intake between groups, and both groups ingested Zn above dietary reference intakes (9.5 mg/day). Levels in biological samples were measured by ICP-MS.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Essential trace mineral crucial for numerous physiological processes, overall health, and athletic function.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Monitored as part of an observational study of male and female soccer players over a regular season, considering its role in overall Zn status and potential influence on other measured Zn compartments.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Serves as an indicator of nutritional status; consistent adequate intake suggests that observed variations in biological compartments are likely due to physiological responses to training rather than dietary deficiency.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Measured at multiple time points; differences to be identified by one-way ANOVA. Specific quantitative changes not provided in the extracted data.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Regulation of the female reproductive system and menstrual cycle.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Observed in female soccer players over a regular season, with measurements taken at multiple time points, specifically considering the menstrual cycle phase to minimize confounding effects on other biomarkers.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reflects female physiological and reproductive status, crucial for contextualizing other biomarker changes (e.g., Zn) and understanding overall health status in female athletes, especially in relation to their menstrual cycle.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Measured at multiple time points; differences to be identified by one-way ANOVA. Specific quantitative changes not provided in the extracted data.
